property_summary: For any nonnegative ETH deposit amount sent to C.receive by any caller, the reference contract always increments depositsCount (so depositsCount after receive >= 1), but the mutant prevents increments once depositsCount is nonzero (failing for some inputs where depositsCount was already nonzero).

For any caller and any nonzero ETH value sent to receive, the reference C always increments depositsCount (so depositsCount after the call is strictly greater than before); the mutant rejects deposits once depositsCount is nonzero, so there exist inputs (a caller sending ETH when depositsCount>0) where the mutant leaves depositsCount unchanged and thus violates this rule.

For any caller sending a positive ETH value to C.receive, the reference contract always increases depositsCount (so depositsCount after the call > depositsCount before); the mutant rejects further deposits once depositsCount is nonzero, so there exist inputs (a caller sending ETH when depositsCount>0) that leave depositsCount unchanged and violate this rule.

For any caller and any nonzero ETH sent to receive, the reference C always makes depositsCount strictly increase (so depositsCount_after >= depositsCount_before + 1 when value>0), whereas the mutant blocks increments when depositsCount was already nonzero, violating this monotonicity for some inputs.

For any caller and any nonzero ETH value, calling receive always makes depositsCount become at least 1 (i.e., depositsCount_after >= 1); the mutant forbids any deposit once depositsCount is nonzero, so there exist inputs (a second deposit) where the mutant leaves depositsCount == 1 while the reference would have increased it further (violating the >=1-after-deposit rule when starting from zero and then depositing again).

For any caller and any nonnegative ether amount, sending ether to C via its receive() always succeeds (does not revert) and increases depositsCount by 1; the mutant that requires false causes receive to always revert for some inputs (any positive value), breaking this rule.

For any caller and any nonnegative ether amount, calling C.receive payable succeeds and increments depositsCount (reference); the mutant makes receive always revert (so for some amounts the call fails and depositsCount does not increase).

For every externally-owned caller and any nonzero ETH value sent to C via its receive fallback, the reference contract accepts the payment and increases depositsCount by 1; the mutant's receive always reverts (require(false)) so some inputs (any positive value) will cause the receive to revert and not increase depositsCount.

For every caller address and any positive ETH amount, sending that amount to C via its receive() completes successfully and increases depositsCount by exactly 1; the mutant makes receive revert (require(false)) so some sends fail and depositsCount does not increase.

For every caller and every nonzero ETH amount sent to C via its receive, the reference contract's receive always accepts the payment (call succeeds) and thus returns true from a try/catch wrapper; the mutant's receive that has require(false) will cause the call to revert for some inputs (any positive amount), breaking this rule.

For any payable call to receive(), the reference contract never lets depositsCount overflow (i.e., depositsCount after the call is >= previous depositsCount), while the mutant that removed the require can allow depositsCount to decrease when depositsCount overflows (wraps) for some input amount causing overflow.

For any single payable call to receive() the depositsCount in the correct contract never decreases (i.e., new depositsCount >= old depositsCount); removing the require allows a crafted reentrant callee to cause depositsCount to be observed smaller after the call for some inputs.

For any single external caller sending value to C via receive, the reference contract guarantees depositsCount after the call is at least the previous depositsCount (it never decreases because of the checked require), while the mutant without the require can be forced (via a reentrant attacker) to observe a smaller depositsCount after the receive completes for some inputs.

After any single external payable send to C.receive by any caller, the correct contract never decreases depositsCount (depositsCount_after >= depositsCount_before) because it requires (depositsCount+1)>=depositsCount, whereas the mutant that removed the require can allow depositsCount to decrease for some inputs (e.g., via overflow), so there exist inputs where depositsCount_after < depositsCount_before.

For every single call to receive() by any caller sending a nonzero ether amount, the reference contract guarantees depositsCount increases by exactly 1 (depositsCount_after == depositsCount_before + 1); the mutant that removed the require can be re-entered by a malicious recipient during the low-level external call in sendMoney to make depositsCount not increase by exactly 1 for some inputs, so there exist fuzzed inputs where depositsCount_after != depositsCount_before + 1 on the mutant.

For any received payment the contract's public depositsCount is non-decreasing (it increases or stays the same); the mutant that decrements depositsCount on receive can make depositsCount decrease for some input amount/sender.
For any caller and any payment amount, calling receive() never decreases depositsCount (it is non-decreasing); the mutant that decrements on receive can make depositsCount smaller for some call.

For any single payable call to receive() from any sender with any nonzero value, depositsCount increases by exactly 1 (i.e. depositsCount_after == depositsCount_before + 1); the mutant that decrements will violate this for some inputs where depositsCount_after != depositsCount_before + 1.

For any caller and any nonzero ether value sent to the contract's receive (via a payable low-level call), the reference implementation ensures depositsCount does not decrease (depositsCount_after >= depositsCount_before); the mutant that decrements on receive can make depositsCount decrease for some inputs.

For any sender and any value, after a payable call to receive(), depositsCount either stays the same when value==0 or increases by 1 when value>0; the mutant that decrements on receive will violate this by producing depositsCount_after < depositsCount_before for some fuzzed sender/value where value>0.

For every single payable call to receive, depositsCount increases by exactly 1 (the reference increments by one per receive); the mutant that increments twice breaks this invariant for some input amounts/senders.

For any single successful external payment to C via its receive (any sender and any nonzero value), depositsCount increases by exactly 1; the mutant that increments twice can make depositsCount increase by 2 for some input, violating this rule.
Only the owner (deployer of C) can successfully call withdrawAll; non-owners cannot withdraw the contract balance.
Calls to withdrawAll initiated by the contract owner must not revert (i.e., owner can withdrawAll).
If the caller is the owner, withdrawAll should not revert.
General rule: if the caller is the owner, withdrawAll should not revert.
If the caller is the owner, withdrawAll should not revert.

For all callers and amounts, when a non-owner address is used as the target of sendMoney(...) the reference contract does not transfer Ether out of the contract (so address(c).balance remains unchanged after the call when sender is owner), but the mutated contract (which inverted onlyOwner) can be made to transfer out funds by calling sendMoney via the owner account — the mutant allows a non-owner-only guard to be bypassed causing differing contract balance behavior for some inputs.

For every caller and target, when the contract's owner calls sendMoney the contract preserves its balance (owner-only functions cannot be used to make the contract send funds to an arbitrary callee); the mutant inverts the ownership check so some inputs (owner as sender with a malicious target) allow the contract to send funds and thus change address(c).balance.

For all caller addresses and target addresses and amounts, when the contract owner calls sendMoney the contract does not transfer out any Ether (so address(c).balance remains unchanged); the mutant inverts the ownership check allowing non-owners to call and can cause the contract balance to decrease for some inputs.

For every target contract and amount, when the contract owner calls sendMoney the reference C never decreases address(c).balance (it will not send funds out), but the mutant that inverts onlyOwner allows some owner-invoked sendMoney calls to transfer Ether out, decreasing address(c).balance.

For any caller and any target, when the contract owner invokes sendMoney the call will NOT succeed in transferring Ether out (address(c).balance remains unchanged); the mutant inverting onlyOwner allows non-owners to call and so there exist inputs (owner as caller combined with a malicious target) that make the mutant change address(c).balance and thus violate this rule.

For any caller who is the owner and any contract balance, calling withdrawAll transfers the entire contract balance to the owner (leaving address(c).balance == 0); the mutant using transfer instead of calling withdraw(...) can break this when the low-level call path in the reference succeeds but transfer reverts (e.g. when the owner is a contract whose payable receive reverts), causing differing post-call balances.

For any recipient contract that may revert on plain transfer(), the correct contract C always leaves address(c).balance == 0 after withdrawAll() (because it calls withdraw which performs a low-level call that returns false but is ignored), whereas the mutant using payable(msg.sender).transfer(...) will revert and leave address(c).balance > 0 (or cause revert) for some recipient contracts — so there exists a recipient and funding amount where withdrawAll succeeds on the reference and fails (or leaves balance unchanged) on the mutant.

For every recipient contract whose fallback/receive ALWAYS REVERTS, the reference C's withdrawAll (which calls withdraw(... ) that uses a low-level .call and ignores the return) will NOT revert when the owner is that contract and will reduce address(c).balance to 0 after success; the mutant using payable(msg.sender).transfer(...) will revert (or leave balance > 0) for some funding amounts — so the invariant is: after owner-invoked withdrawAll by a reverting recipient-owner, the reference leaves address(c).balance == 0 while the mutant can fail and leave balance > 0.

For any owner that is an EOA, withdrawAll always empties the contract balance (address(c).balance == 0) after the call; the mutant using transfer can revert when the owner is a contract with a gas-consuming receive (or when gas stipends cause transfer to revert), so there exist inputs (a contract-owner with payable receive consuming gas) where the reference succeeds but the mutant reverts or leaves balance > 0.

For any owner contract with a failing payable receive, the reference C's withdrawAll (which routes through withdraw using low-level .call and ignores its return) does not revert and leaves address(c).balance == 0 after the owner invokes it; the mutant using payable(msg.sender).transfer(...) will revert (or fail) for some owner contracts/amounts, violating that property.

For any caller who is owner and when the contract has a positive balance, calling withdrawAll transfers the contract's entire ETH balance to the owner (reference); the mutant calls withdraw(0) and thus can leave the contract balance unchanged for some inputs.

For any caller who is the owner and any positive contract balance funded by that owner, calling withdrawAll always reduces address(c).balance to zero (reference); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave address(c).balance > 0 for some inputs, violating this rule.

For any owner caller and any nonzero contract balance funded by that owner, calling withdrawAll reduces the contract balance to zero (reference) while the mutant calling withdraw(0) can leave the contract balance > 0.
For any owner caller and any nonzero contract balance, calling withdrawAll transfers all ETH out so address(c).balance becomes zero; the mutant calling withdraw(0) can leave address(c).balance > 0.

For any owner caller and any positive contract balance funded by that owner, calling withdrawAll causes the contract balance to become zero (reference); the mutant calls withdraw(0) and can leave the contract balance > 0 for some inputs.

For any caller who is the owner and any contract balance, calling withdrawAll always reduces the contract balance to zero in the reference C (because it calls withdraw which transfer-reverts on failure), but the mutant that uses sendMoney (low-level call) can leave non-zero balance when the callee reverts or otherwise causes the low-level call to fail silently.

For any owner caller and any prior deposits, calling withdrawAll always reduces the contract balance to zero (reference uses transfer which reverts on failure); the mutant using low-level call may leave a non-zero contract balance when the recipient's fallback reverts or otherwise causes the call to fail silently.

For any recipient address that may revert on receiving funds, the reference contract's withdrawAll (which uses transfer via withdraw) always leaves the contract balance at zero after a successful call by the owner, whereas the mutant (which uses a low-level call in sendMoney) can complete withdrawAll while leaving a non-zero contract balance when the recipient's fallback reverts (low-level call failure is ignored).

For any owner caller and any recipient contract that reverts in its fallback/receive, the reference C's withdrawAll call (which uses transfer via withdraw) will revert and thus not leave funds in C, whereas the mutant that uses low-level call via sendMoney can complete withdrawAll while leaving C's balance nonzero; therefore the property: withdrawAll either reverts (ok==false) OR leaves address(c).balance == 0 — the reference always reverts for a reverting recipient (so ok==false) but the mutant can return ok==true with nonzero balance.
